messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Forester
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Pain): Physical pain in a part of the body, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Proximity: Physical proximity
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# James

James was forty-two when the chainsaw kicked back. He had been working the northeastern ridge of the Monongahela National Forest for seventeen years, and he knew the weight of equipment the way other men know their own breath. The morning had been clear, the crew in good spirits, and the stand of diseased hemlock was coming down exactly as planned. His colleague Marcus had moved in to help clear a bind, positioning himself just where James had calculated he would not be—where the kickback, when it came, would miss him by inches. But the blade caught the grain differently than James had anticipated. In the fraction of a second between the machine's violent reversal and Marcus's scream, James understood with absolute clarity that he had made the miscalculation. The chainsaw caught Marcus's left leg just above the knee. The blood came fast. The helicopter ride to the trauma center took forty minutes, and James sat in the cabin knowing, with the certainty of a man who had just watched his own negligence made flesh, that he had broken something in Marcus that no surgery could fully repair. Marcus lost the leg below the knee. He never came back to forestry.

For months afterward, James continued working. He told himself that stopping would be worse—that he needed to reclaim the ridge, to prove that one mistake did not define twelve years of safe practice. But something had shifted in his relationship to the work itself. When he caught the scent of fresh-cut wood or felt the particular strain in his shoulders that came from holding a chainsaw at the precise angle required for a clean fell, his body would flood with a sensation he could only describe as falling. His chest would tighten, his hands would shake on the controls, and he would be back in that moment of miscalculation, feeling the exact posture he had held—the slight forward lean, the grip, the weight distribution—as if his body were being forced to relive the geometry of his own failure. The physical sensations became inextricable from the memory itself. Even on days when he was not cutting, a sharp pain in his own left shoulder—an old injury, nothing serious—would suddenly transport him backward, and with it came the memory, vivid and embodied, of that morning on the ridge.

What frightened James most was not the memory itself, but what the memory proved about him. He had come to believe that the accident revealed something intrinsic, some flaw in his judgment or his character that had always been there, waiting for the right circumstance to destroy someone else's life. He could not rely on himself anymore. How could he, when the evidence was so clear? He began to notice threats everywhere. In the grocery store, a stranger reaching past him for a can would send his eyes tracking the man's hands, searching for hostile intent where none existed. At home, when a neighbor stopped by to chat, James found himself studying the man's face, trying to read whether this person harbored some grievance, some reason to wish him harm. His wife, Sarah, had begun to mention that he seemed different—more distant, more watchful. He told her he was fine, but the truth was that he could not relax, not even in their living room with the doors locked and Sarah beside him. His body remained in a state of constant vigilance, as if the accident had rewired something fundamental in how he perceived the world.

The physical pain in his shoulder, the memory of that morning, and his new conviction that he was fundamentally unsafe—these had begun to feed each other. When his shoulder ached, the memory would surface, and with it the rage and grief that accompanied the recollection of what he had done. That rage and grief would crystallize into the conviction that he was incapable, that he could no longer trust his own judgment, that he was a danger to anyone who worked beside him. This certainty led him to withdraw from the crew, to volunteer for solo assignments, to spend more time in the office doing paperwork than in the field doing the work that had once defined him. His supervisor had noticed. There had been a quiet conversation about his fitness for the job. James had not fought it. He had come to believe, with the weight of absolute truth, that the best thing he could do for anyone was to remove himself from situations where his flawed judgment might cause harm again. By the time he walked into the therapist's office, he had been on modified duty for eight months, was sleeping poorly, had lost twenty pounds, and could not remember the last time he had felt anything other than the dull ache of his own culpability. What he wanted most was to stop feeling like a danger. What he feared most was that he never would.
